paragraphs: I studied abroad for three months at the University of Adelaide in Australia and did my clerkship at the Women's and Children's Hospital (WCH) in the city of Adelaide. Adelaide is not that large a city, but it is surrounded by rich nature and was a very pleasant place to live.

The WCH, where I spent the three-month clerkship, is a specialist hospital for pediatrics and obstetrics, and patients come from all over South Australia. I rotated through one department every two weeks and did clerkships in Allergy/Immunology, Genetics, Infectious Disease, Respiratory and Neurology. On the first day of the clerkship, the person in charge had completely forgotten that I was coming, and the clerkship departments were somehow decided on the spot after searching around the hospital, but as a result I was able to have very good experiences in every department.

In Allergy/Immunology, where I rotated for the first two weeks and the last two weeks, the student's job in the Medical Day Unit was to take histories and perform physical examinations of patients and report to the Registrar. Sometimes I was casually instructed, "Write up the prescription, I'll sign it later," which was a surprise for me, who was used to clerkships in Japan. In the first two weeks my history taking and presentations did not go as I wished and I was quite depressed, but when I did the clerkship in the last two weeks I could take histories and present better than before, and I was happy about the small growth. In Genetics I examined patients with rare genetic diseases and was allowed to sit in on counseling. I missed about three days in the middle because of influenza, which was unfortunate, but the doctors were kind and it was very educational. In the Infectious Disease department, I was able to see rare cases such as osteomyelitis and ventriculoperitoneal shunt infection, which I had had little contact with in Japan. I also did history taking, physical examination and presentations together with the students and was stunned at the difference in ability from the students. In Respiratory, I was able to see many cases of Cystic Fibrosis, which is rare in Japan. I followed rounds, was allowed to do physical examinations and observed the outpatient clinic, and it was quite fulfilling. In Neurology, I was able to see a wide range of cases, including cerebral palsy, epilepsy and MELAS. Surprisingly, outpatient appointments in this department had a wait of up to two years, and I felt the difference from Japan's healthcare system.

In addition to the clerkship in each department, I took part in various teaching sessions together with fifth-year students at the University of Adelaide. In the teaching sessions, a supervising doctor is assigned to a group of several students, and they do history taking, physical examination and presentations and receive feedback. In addition, I had many opportunities to interact with students, in classes and emergency training, and was able to learn about differences in medical education and so on. There were also many exchange students from Asia, and I found the differences from their home countries interesting. It is also a good memory that students I became friends with invited me to meals and we had fun playing mahjong together.

Honestly, I was very anxious before departure and not confident that I could finish the clerkship. However, supported by the students and doctors of the University of Adelaide, the university's administrative staff and the doctors of the International Collaboration Office, I was able to finish the clerkship safely. Being able to stay and do a clerkship in an environment very different from Japan, in healthcare system, cultural background and racial diversity, is an irreplaceable experience for me.
